findings.location: sections/30-call-to-the-nations.tex, subsection 'Two difficulties: the burned city, and St Gregory's highways', final paragraph (lines 293-303): 'A third answer comes from outside the Fathers. Honorius Augustodunensis reads the Introit, Collect, Epistle, Gradual, Offertory and Communion of this Mass, which his own book shares ... His reading makes the formulary a homecoming rather than a mission. ...'
findings.problem: Honorius's Mass for these chants (Gemma animae IV.86) had another Alleluia (Dextera Dei, Ps 117:16) and another Gospel (Mt 9, the paralytic), as research/scope.md sections 2.1 and 3.12 record. The paragraph nonetheless sets his return-from-exile reading of six shared elements as 'a third answer' to this reading's own question (who was called, what became of the call, what the highways are) and says that 'His reading makes the formulary a homecoming rather than a mission'. The mission it is set against is built from this formulary's Alleluia and Gospel, neither of which stood in his Mass, so the sentence credits him with a reading of this formulary, and with an answer about the call and the highways, that he never gave. guidance/liturgy/propers-three-documents.md ('Liturgical commentators') lets such a commentator be cited only for what he says of an element this formulary shares, never in relation to this formulary's Gospel, and keeps his other Mass out of the readings; the clause 'which his own book shares' points the reader to that other Mass inside the reading. The proper-study contract also forbids representing a witness's exegesis as his synthesis of this Mass.
findings.required_result: Honorius is cited in this reading only for what he says of the shared elements, as the element-by-element section already does. Either the paragraph leaves the difficulties subsection, or it is recast so that its subject is the shared chants and prayers alone (for example, that he hears them as the prayer of a people on its way home), with no 'third answer', no claim about 'the formulary', no contrast with the mission carried by the Alleluia and the Gospel, and no allusion to what his book does not share.

findings.location: sections/80-date-location.tex, Gospel dossier (summary row 'Event: Jerusalem, in the temple ...' and explanatory row 'Traditional attribution: St Matthew the Apostle ... all marked disputed and none preferred. The Location column gives the place of the narrated event, not of the writing.') and Epistle dossier (summary row 'Paul, a prisoner in the Lord (4:1), to the saints who are at Ephesus (1:1)' and explanatory row 'Traditional attribution: St Paul ... The record marks both disputed.'); sections/90-apparatus.tex, 'Chronology' paragraph ('For the Gospel and the Epistle it holds the traditional dates reported by the Catholic Encyclopedia, every one marked disputed.')
findings.problem: (1) The Gospel's generated Date cell lists six composition dates, the last 'c. A.D. 50'. In the declared chronology evidence (src/sources/chronology/composition.yaml, composition.gospel-of-matthew, the claim drawn from Durand's 'The New Testament'), that is Durand's date for the lost Aramaic original: the entry quotes his next sentence, 'We know nothing definite of the date of its being rendered into Greek', and warns that 'A consumer that reads it as the date of the Greek Matthew is reading it wrongly.' The same entry reports the tradition behind the earlier dates, that 'Matthew wrote his Gospel in Hebrew when he left Palestine' (Eusebius, as the Catholic Encyclopedia reports him). The explanatory row calls all six 'traditional Catholic dates that disagree with one another' for the Gospel's composition and says nothing of the Hebrew original or of what c. A.D. 50 dates, and the scope appendix repeats it; a reader of this row, and of the concise page 2 that must reprint it, takes c. A.D. 50 as a date of the Gospel as it is read. (2) The 1962 dossier rule (guidance/liturgy/roman-1962-propers.md, 'Page 2: Scriptural date and location') requires the composition place and first audience and the distinction of writer, event and recipient geography. The Gospel row gives only the event's place and says outright that the place of writing is not given, although the entry above supplies the tradition of the writing. The Epistle row names the recipients at Ephesus and the chains but no place of writing, although the declared entry composition.epistle-to-the-ephesians gives Ladeuze's statement that whether the captivity letters were produced 'in Caesarea or in Rome ... is still a much mooted question', and Prat's table sets the letter within the captivity at Rome. guidance/liturgy/propers-three-documents.md makes this appendix the reviewed home that the concise page 2 must draw on and may not supplement.
findings.required_result: From the declared chronology evidence, and without printing any date that research/chronology.toml does not hold, the Gospel's explanatory row gives the tradition of the Gospel's writing (in Hebrew, when Matthew left Palestine, as Eusebius is reported) and states that c. A.D. 50 is Durand's date for the Aramaic original, the date of its Greek rendering being unknown to him. The Epistle's row gives the place of writing as its source gives it: a captivity at Caesarea or at Rome, which Ladeuze calls a much mooted question, with Prat's table placing the letter in the Roman captivity. The scope appendix's Chronology paragraph agrees with both rows. The Date cells remain the generated annotations.

findings.location: sections/00-opening.tex, lines 75-81 ('... and St Augustine, St Gregory, St John Chrysostom and Bl. Ildefonso Schuster carry it: the feast is the Church now, at the Lord's table, where the King comes in to see his guests'); sections/40-feast-that-now-is.tex, opening paragraph and 'Two feasts' subsection; sections/50-comparison.tex, comparison table row 'Carried by'; proper-components.toml, lane feast-that-now-is, carrying_authors
findings.problem: Schuster's own comment on this Gospel (The Sacramentary III, p. 173; research/scope.md section 3.6) reads the parable's banquet as 'the heavenly banquet' to which souls are predestined, not as the Church now at table. The opening nevertheless names him among those who 'carry it: the feast is the Church now, at the Lord's table', and nothing in the third reading records his different reading of the feast, although guidance/liturgy/propers-three-documents.md requires the authors who carry a reading to agree on its controlling claims and any narrower disagreement to be preserved beside the relevant claim. The reading's own introduction states his role correctly (he reads the Gradual, Secret and Postcommunion 'in the same direction'), so the opening's colon puts in his mouth the one claim he does not make, and the manifest and the comparison then list him as a carrier of it.
findings.required_result: The opening credits the identification of the feast with the present Church to the witnesses who make it (Augustine and Gregory, with Chrysostom's address to those who have partaken of the mysteries) and states Schuster's contribution as what it is: his reading of this Mass's Gradual, Secret and Postcommunion. If Schuster remains a carrying author of feast-that-now-is, the reading records beside its claim about the feast that his own comment on the Gospel speaks of souls predestined 'to the heavenly banquet'. Otherwise he leaves that lane's carrying_authors and the comparison's 'Carried by' cell; Augustine, Gregory and Chrysostom already satisfy the standing rule.

findings.location: sections/80-date-location.tex, explanatory rows: 'The chronology record holds no traditional date for the psalm' (Introit); 'the record dates neither that occasion nor the psalm' (Alleluia); 'The record holds no traditional date for the psalm' (Communion); 'The record assigns the psalm no Davidic era' (Offertory); 'the record assigns no Davidic era' (Gradual); 'the record gives the episode no date', 'all marked disputed and none preferred', 'The Location column gives the place of the narrated event' (Gospel); 'The record marks both disputed' (Epistle); and the Location cells of the five psalm dossiers
findings.problem: Every explanatory row makes the leaf's own research record, or the table's own column, the grammatical subject and reports evidence-state labels ('marked disputed', 'none preferred'). guidance/liturgy/roman-1962-propers.md names Scriptural Date and Location among the sections both house-voice rules reach, and guidance/editorial.md counts the guide's own apparatus as a subject among the forms of the defect. Separately, the psalms' Location cells describe each psalm's content rather than any setting or place; the Communion's is 'The first strophe, Aleph, of the psalm of the law'. This appendix is the text the concise page 2 will be drawn from, so its register will travel with it.
findings.required_result: Each row states its finding with a source or a fact as subject (for example: the NABRE introduction to the Psalms places the Psalter's completion before the Maccabean period and holds that no psalm can be dated securely; the Catholic Encyclopedia's dates for Matthew disagree and it settles on none), keeping every limit the rows now carry. The psalms' Location cells give a setting or orientation, or the traditional attribution by title, rather than genre or strophe.

findings.location: sections/10-each-element.tex against sections/40-feast-that-now-is.tex (Schuster on the Introit, Collect, Gradual, Secret and Postcommunion; the Latin of Ps 140:2 at Ordo Missae no. 1037); sections/20-wedding-garment.tex, 'What God commands is asked of God: the other elements' (Schuster on the Secret); sections/30-call-to-the-nations.tex, 'The other elements on the way', against sections/40-feast-that-now-is.tex, 'The evening sacrifice: St Augustine on the Gradual' (Augustine, Enarr. 140, 2)
findings.problem: The same quotations are printed in full two or three times. Schuster's Secret sentence ('such dispositions as may enable the mystical sacramental oblation to exert without hindrance its full power in our souls') appears three times; his sentences on the Introit, Collect, Gradual and Postcommunion appear twice each, in the element section and again in the third reading; Augustine's 'if tribulation remain for the Church, for the Body of Christ, even to the end of the world ...' appears in both the second and the third reading; and the Latin of the incensation (Ps 140:2-4, Ordo Missae no. 1037) is printed twice. guidance/liturgy/propers-three-documents.md asks each substantial argument to have one fullest home, and guidance/liturgy/roman-1962-propers.md asks for repeated quotations to be removed.
findings.required_result: Each of these quotations is printed once, where it does the most work, and referred to briefly elsewhere; each reading keeps its argument.

findings.location: sections/40-feast-that-now-is.tex, subsection 'Commanded and asked, healed and held: the Communion and the Postcommunion', second paragraph ('Chrysostom, Gregory and Hilary use the same language of healing in other places, though none of them comments on this prayer. ...')
findings.problem: Only Chrysostom's evening psalm as a 'saving medicine' is healing language. Gregory's 'remedia vitae vestrae' are what the deaths of the fathers offer the hearers for their own lives (Hom. 38, 4), and Hilary's 'infirmes per naturam nostram' names nature's weakness without God's direction (Tract. in Ps. 118, Aleph 12); neither speaks of a healing work. The sentence presents a shared vocabulary the witnesses do not have, which is the name list and stretched link that guidance/liturgy/roman-1962-propers.md tells a commentary to remove, and it adds nothing that the Postcommunion's own words and Schuster do not already give the reading.
findings.required_result: Drop the list, or keep only what a witness says in the language of healing, attributed to its own object; the Postcommunion's contribution rests on its text and on Schuster.

findings.location: (a) sections/05-appointed-texts.tex, Collect note, 'The Collect is the only oration of the Mass'; (b) sections/10-each-element.tex, Offertory subsection, 'remembers that God heard him "In what day soever I shall call upon thee" (v. 3)'; (c) sections/10-each-element.tex, Gradual subsection, last sentence, 'The Fathers read the verse's evening sacrifice in sharply different ways'; (d) sections/40-feast-that-now-is.tex, 'The table is not the garment', first paragraph, 'St Gregory's warning, "look carefully, brethren, lest the king coming in find fault with anything in the dress of your mind"'; (e) sections/90-apparatus.tex, Reception, 'expounded a Mass that shared this formulary's chants and Epistle but read another Gospel'
findings.problem: (a) The same section calls the Collect, Secret and Postcommunion 'the three orations'; the sentence means that no other collect is added, but it says the Mass has one oration. (b) In the Vulgate and the Douay, Ps 137:3 is a petition ('hear me'), and the Introit subsection rightly calls it a prayer; the memory of being heard is v. 1 ('for thou hast heard the words of my mouth'). (c) Two Fathers are meant, and the third reading itself says their two answers 'are not opposed in doctrine'; 'The Fathers ... sharply different' overstates a difference the study elsewhere measures exactly. (d) The quoted English is the study's own gloss of Gregory's Latin, set in quotation marks as his words far from the Latin; research/scope.md section 6 takes a Father's English only from a named translation and otherwise quotes the Latin. (e) Honorius's and Durandus's Mass also had another Alleluia (research/scope.md section 3.12), and Berno's is recorded as sharing only the Introit, Collect and Epistle, so 'shared this formulary's chants' overstates.
findings.required_result: (a) Say that the Collect is said alone, with no other oration added. (b) Describe v. 3 as the prayer it is, or attach the memory of being heard to v. 1. (c) Name Augustine and Hilary and state the difference without 'sharply'. (d) Quote Gregory's Latin, or paraphrase him without quotation marks. (e) Keep the one permitted clause, worded so that it is true of each commentator (for example, a Mass that shared some of this formulary's chants and read another Gospel).

observations.location: sections/80-date-location.tex, Gospel and Epistle explanatory rows; src/sources/chronology/composition.yaml, entries composition.gospel-of-matthew and composition.epistle-to-the-ephesians
observations.note: guidance/liturgy/roman-1962-propers.md requires the principal modern critical horizon in each page-2 explanatory row ('required rather than tolerated'), but the chronology corpus holds no modern critical claim for Matthew or Ephesians (its Matthew entry sets the critics the Catholic Encyclopedia lists aside as 'no part of this profile'), so neither this appendix nor the concise page 2 can carry one; research/scope.md section 10.5 lists the psalms' missing traditional attributions and the Gospel's undated event as open corpus work but not this gap, and no gate checks the requirement.

summary: Reviewed the expansive study of liturgy/roman-rite/1962/propers/temporal/59-nineteenth-after-pentecost (main.tex and its nine components; author proof 33 pages, SHA-256 b52d7820...) against the proper-study contract, the three-document and 1962 profiles, the sealed research records and the tracked source texts; every sealed input matched its REVIEW_INPUTS hash. Checked: the appointed Latin against propers/verified.md and the Clementine; every English quotation against the tracked Douay, Cummiskey, NPNF 1-6/1-8/1-10/1-13, ANF 1, Bellarmine, Schuster and Liturgical Year texts; the Latin of Gregory (Hom. 38), Augustine (Enarr. 104, Quaest. ev. I.31), Hilary (PL 9 layer), Aquinas (1857 layer) and Jerome (PL 26, Internet Archive text layer); section and page loci; and the rubrical claims against research/context.md. All quotations match their sources. The three readings are distinct, coherent, carried by developed patristic arguments, engage every element and close with their own four senses; the comparison is truthful. Three study-owned defects block: Honorius, whose Mass had another Gospel and Alleluia, is presented as a 'third answer' reading of this formulary (STU-001); the Gospel and Epistle dossiers omit writer geography and the Aramaic-original qualification that the declared chronology evidence supplies (STU-002); and the opening credits Schuster with the present-Church reading of the feast, which he does not hold (STU-003). Four advisories and one observation on the corpus's missing NT critical horizon follow. Limits: the PG 27/PG 55 Greek and the medieval commentators were checked against the research records, not re-read; rubric loci were checked against research/context.md, not the facsimile; the PDF was checked for page count and contents only. Verdict: CHANGES_REQUIRED.
